message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
# Review: Feasibility Study, Weekly Food Waste Collection

**Summary:** The cost table adds up correctly, and the pilot is a real strength. But the study's three main conclusions are each contradicted by its own figures:

- **Participation in flats was a third of the rate in houses, not "broadly similar."**
- **The projection uses a 64% participation rate that appears nowhere in the pilot data.** With the pilot's actual figures, the net cost rises to about £521,000, which exceeds the £520,000 allocation.
- **Brookfield can take only 1,800 tonnes a year**, well short of the projected tonnage, so treatment is not all local and its full cost is not in the figures.

As written, the conclusions that the scheme is "uniform" and "fully funded" don't hold.

## 1. Participation was not similar across housing types

| Housing type | Participation |
|---|---|
| Houses | 66% |
| Flats | **21%** |

This is the biggest gap in the pilot, and the study draws the opposite conclusion from it. Flats are about 20% of the district (around 10,400 households). The data argue *for* a separate approach to flats, such as communal bins, bin-store caddies, targeted engagement or different collection points. They don't support "a single, simple service" without one. The recommendation and the author's description both need to change.

## 2. The 64% participation rate isn't in the data

The pilot's overall rate was **57%** (2,280 ÷ 4,000), and the pilot's housing mix (20% flats) matches the district's. So 57% is the figure to use, ideally applied separately to each housing type:

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | ≈ 2,710 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | ≈ 160 |
| **Total** | | | | **≈ 2,870** |

That's about 2,870 tonnes, against the study's 3,290, which is about 13% less. Consequences:

- The disposal saving falls from about £243,000 to about **£212,500** (2,870 × £74).
- The net cost rises from about £490,000 to about **£521,000** (£733,400 − £212,500).
- **That's already above the £520,000 allocation**, before the treatment issue below.

If 64% came from somewhere else, such as a later month or a different measure, the study needs to explain it.

## 3. Treatment capacity falls short of the tonnage

Brookfield's contracted capacity is **1,800 tonnes a year until 2029**. Projected tonnage is about 2,870 on the pilot rates, or 3,290 on the study's own figure. That leaves **roughly 1,070–1,490 tonnes a year** with nowhere local to go. The options are:

- **Haul it 46 miles to the next AD plant.** That adds a gate fee that isn't stated, plus haulage or a transfer station, none of which is costed.
- **Keep it in the residual stream.** That cuts the disposal saving to about 1,800 × £74 ≈ £133,000, and undermines compliance.

Even at the lower tonnage, this probably adds tens of thousands of pounds a year. The statement "Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away" is true only for the first 1,800 tonnes. The study should cost a realistic treatment arrangement for 2027 to 2029.

## 4. Funding is provisional, and the margin is already gone

- The £520,000 is a **provisional** allocation that the Government "has indicated" will be provided. The study should say what happens if the confirmed figure is lower, and whether the funding is guaranteed beyond the first year.
- On the pilot figures, the scheme is about £1,000 over the allocation **before** the treatment shortfall and the costs listed below. "Fully funded" should not be in the recommendation unless the gaps are closed.

## 5. Costs that aren't shown

The author describes the analysis as showing "every cost line," but several costs are missing:

- **Overflow treatment and haulage** (see section 3).
- **The dedicated phone line and web page** mentioned in section 6.
- **Recruitment and training** for 12 operatives.
- **Cover for holiday and sickness, supervision and route management.** Six crews with no relief staff is lean.
- **Vehicle finance.** Straight-line depreciation is shown, but no interest or capital financing cost. Also, there are no spare vehicles for breakdowns.
- **The up-front cost of caddies.** They're shown "annualised", but rolling out to 52,000 households in March 2027 means the cash is needed in 2026–27.

## 6. Assumptions to check

- **The incineration saving.** Saving £112 per tonne assumes the incinerator contract charges per tonne with no minimum-tonnage ("put-or-pay") clause. If there is one, diverting waste may save less.
- **Vehicle lead time.** Ordering in December 2026 for delivery in March 2027 assumes about three months. Specialist food waste vehicles often take considerably longer. Confirm a delivery date with suppliers, since the whole timetable depends on it.
- **Crew productivity.** Six vehicles for 52,000 households means about 1,700 households per vehicle per day over a five-day week. Show that this is realistic using pilot round data, especially for village rounds.
- **The pilot season.** January to June misses summer and the Christmas peak, and early enthusiasm may fade. Flag this as a limitation.
- **Statutory timing.** The study says councils are "required to introduce" weekly collections, but proposes starting in April 2027. Under the Simpler Recycling rules, the general deadline for household food waste collections was 31 March 2026, with transitional arrangements for some councils. Confirm whether Thornbury has a transitional arrangement, and state it in the study, because Cabinet will want to know whether the Council is already late.
- **Satisfaction figures.** For the 81% satisfaction rating, give the survey sample size and response rate.

## What holds up

- The vehicle, crew and total cost arithmetic is correct: £990,000 ÷ 7 ≈ £141,400, 12 × £34,000 = £408,000, and the total is £733,400.
- The participation rates in Table 1 are calculated correctly.
- Contamination of under 2% is genuinely good, and so is the fall in missed collections.
- The pilot design, with mixed wards and housing types and weekly measurement, is a real strength. It is what makes the problem with flats visible.
- 5 April 2027 is a Monday and avoids the Easter bank holidays.

## Recommended changes before Cabinet

1. Rewrite the findings on flats and propose and cost a separate approach for them.
2. Use the pilot's actual participation rates, calculated separately for each housing type, and recalculate tonnage, savings and net cost.
3. Cost the treatment of tonnage above Brookfield's 1,800 tonnes until 2029.
4. Add the missing cost lines and show cash flow for the first year, not just annualised figures.
5. Treat funding as provisional, and show the position if the allocation is lower.
6. Confirm the vehicle lead time, the incinerator contract terms and the statutory deadline.
7. Remove "fully funded" and "uniform" from the recommendation unless the revised figures support them.

The case for going ahead may still be strong, since collection is a legal requirement anyway. But Cabinet should approve it knowing the realistic net cost, the gap in treatment capacity, and the extra work needed to make the service work for flats.
